set.detail:
Lucius Septimius Severus was born at Lepcis Magna in Tripolitania on 11 April 145 into a wealthy family of Punic origin that had reached equestrian and then senatorial rank; two relatives had been consuls. He came to Rome under Marcus Aurelius with the help of a kinsman, and a senatorial career followed: quaestor, legate to the proconsul of Africa, tribune of the plebs, praetor (178), commander of legio IV Scythica in Syria, governor of Gallia Lugdunensis (c. 186-189), where, a widower, he married Julia Domna of Emesa because, it was said, her horoscope foretold that she would marry a king, proconsul of Sicily, suffect consul (190) and in 191 legate of Pannonia Superior. The Historia Augusta claims he never lost his African accent.

Proclaimed at Carnuntum on 9 April 193, he won the throne in four years of civil war against Didius Julianus, Pescennius Niger (Cyzicus, Nicaea and Issus, 193-194) and Clodius Albinus (Lugdunum, 197). He sacked Ctesiphon (198), created the province of Mesopotamia, visited Egypt and his native Africa (202-203), where he lavished buildings on Lepcis, and celebrated the Secular Games in 204. His long-dominant praetorian prefect and fellow-African Plautianus fell in 205; thereafter jurists such as Papinian shaped policy. He died at York on 4 February 211 during his Caledonian war.

Severus transformed the monarchy into an openly military regime: higher pay and privileges for soldiers, three new legions, a Guard recruited from the legions, equestrian commanders, and division of provinces to prevent rebellions. He legitimised himself by declaring himself the son of Marcus Aurelius and brother of Commodus, whom he deified. Dio, who knew him, praises his energy and frugality but deplores his cruelty and his favour to soldiers. Gibbon called him the principal author of the decline of the empire; Anthony Birley's biography stresses his ability and the integration of Africa and the east into the ruling class.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Birley, Septimius Severus: The African Emperor (2nd ed., 1988)

set.detail:
Julia Domna was born around 160 at Emesa in Syria, daughter of Julius Bassianus, hereditary high priest of the sun god Elagabal; her name Domna is Arabic or Aramaic. She married Septimius Severus around 187 and gave birth to Caracalla at Lugdunum on 4 April 188 and to Geta at Rome on 7 March 189. As empress she received unprecedented titles: mater castrorum (mother of the camp) in 195, later mater Augusti et Caesaris, senatus et patriae. She accompanied Severus on his eastern campaigns and to Britain, and her portraits, with a distinctive wig of waved hair, were copied across the empire.

Her position was threatened by the praetorian prefect Plautianus, who investigated her for adultery and drove her to study philosophy, until his fall in 205. Philostratus, who wrote his Life of Apollonius of Tyana at her request, speaks of a circle of 'geometers and philosophers' around her; Glen Bowersock warned against exaggerating this 'salon', but she clearly patronised Greek intellectuals. After Severus' death she tried to reconcile her sons and was wounded when Caracalla had Geta killed in her arms in December 211, being forbidden even to mourn.

Under Caracalla she managed much of the imperial correspondence and petitions, especially during his eastern campaign when she stayed at Antioch and Nicomedia, and Dio says the emperor ignored her advice. When she learned of his murder in April 217, Julia, suffering from breast cancer and unwilling to return to private life under Macrinus, starved herself to death at Antioch. She was deified under Elagabalus. Her sister Julia Maesa and nieces Julia Soaemias and Julia Mamaea later placed Elagabalus and Severus Alexander on the throne, making the Syrian women the real continuity of the Severan dynasty.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Levick, Julia Domna: Syrian Empress (2007)
Bowersock, Greek Sophists in the Roman Empire (1969)

set.detail:
Born Lucius Septimius Bassianus at Lugdunum on 4 April 188, he was renamed Marcus Aurelius Antoninus in 195, when his father claimed descent from Marcus Aurelius, and became Caesar in 196 and Augustus at the age of ten in 198. The nickname Caracalla came from a hooded Gallic cloak he made fashionable. In 202 he was married to Plautianus' daughter Plautilla, whom he hated; after her father's fall in 205 she was exiled and later killed. He campaigned with his father in Britain and, after Severus' death in 211, ruled jointly with Geta until he had him murdered in December 211, followed by a purge of perhaps 20,000 people.

Caracalla's reign is best known for the Constitutio Antoniniana (212), which made almost all free inhabitants of the empire citizens, the vast baths that bear his name (dedicated 216), the new antoninianus coin (215) and a fifty per cent pay rise for the army, whose favour he cultivated by sharing the soldiers' rations and labour. In 213 he campaigned against the Alamanni, the first mention of that people in Dio, and then went east, obsessed with Alexander the Great: he styled himself a new Alexander, formed a Macedonian phalanx and wore Macedonian dress. At Alexandria in 215, angered by the citizens' mockery, he massacred young men and others. In 216 he invaded Parthia, desecrating the royal tombs at Arbela.

He was murdered near Carrhae on 8 April 217 at the instigation of his prefect Macrinus. The soldiers mourned him and forced his deification. Dio, a senator who suffered under him, and Herodian depict a paranoid, cruel tyrant; his portraits, with a scowling, head-turning pose, deliberately project military ferocity. Modern historians stress his popularity with the army and the long-term significance of the citizenship grant.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Kühnen, Die Imitatio Alexandri in der römischen Politik (2008)

set.detail:
Varius Avitus Bassianus was born around 203-204 at Emesa, son of Julia Soaemias and the Syrian senator Sextus Varius Marcellus, and great-nephew of Julia Domna. As a boy he became high priest of the sun god Elagabal, worshipped in the form of a conical black stone. After Caracalla's death his grandmother Julia Maesa, with her eunuch adviser Gannys and the officer Eutychianus, spread the story that he was Caracalla's natural son and had him proclaimed by legio III Gallica at Raphanea on 16 May 218. Macrinus was defeated near Antioch on 8 June. The new emperor, officially Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, travelled slowly to Rome, arriving in 219, and had a portrait of himself in priestly robes hung in the Senate house so that senators would become used to it.

He placed Elagabal above Jupiter, building the Elagabalium on the Palatine and a summer temple outside the city, and staged a midsummer procession in which he ran backwards before the god's chariot. He married five times, including twice to the Vestal Julia Aquilia Severa, and joined the god to Pallas and then to the Carthaginian goddess Caelestis. Dio and Herodian describe his public 'marriage' to the charioteer Hierocles and his favours to the athlete Zoticus, and Dio claims that he asked doctors to give him female genitals; these reports, from hostile sources, have recently been read in terms of gender identity, though they may be invective.

Maesa, seeing his unpopularity, had him adopt his cousin Alexianus, renamed Severus Alexander, as Caesar in 221. When Elagabalus tried to remove him, the Praetorians killed Elagabalus and his mother in their camp in March 222, dragged the bodies through the city and threw them into the Tiber; his name was erased. The Historia Augusta's life is largely fiction. Martijn Icks' study shows how his image as the archetypal decadent was constructed.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Icks, The Crimes of Elagabalus (2011)

set.detail:
Gessius Bassianus Alexianus was born on 1 October 208 at Arca Caesarea in Phoenicia, son of Julia Mamaea and the equestrian Gessius Marcianus. Adopted by his cousin Elagabalus in 221 and renamed Marcus Aurelius Severus Alexander, he became emperor at thirteen after Elagabalus' murder in March 222. Government was effectively in the hands of his grandmother Julia Maesa until her death (c. 224-226) and then of his mother, with a council of senators and jurists, including Ulpian as praetorian prefect, who was murdered by the Guard in 223. Cassius Dio, consul with Alexander in 229, was advised to spend his consulship outside Rome because the Praetorians hated him.

The Historia Augusta presents Alexander as an ideal emperor, respectful of the Senate, who kept statues of Christ, Abraham, Orpheus and Apollonius in his private chapel; this picture is largely fiction. Herodian portrays a mild, well-meaning youth dominated by his avaricious mother. Mamaea is said to have summoned Origen to Antioch to discuss religion. Alexander married Sallustia Orbiana in 225, but her father was executed and she was exiled in 227.

The rise of Sasanian Persia forced Alexander east. Ardashir invaded Mesopotamia in 230; Alexander's three-pronged counter-offensive of 232 achieved partial success with heavy losses, and he celebrated a triumph in 233. Germanic attacks on the Rhine and Danube called him west in 234. At Mogontiacum he preferred negotiation and payment to battle, which alienated the army, and in March 235 soldiers led by Maximinus killed him and his mother at Vicus Britannicus. He was 26. His death ended the Severan dynasty and is the traditional start of the crisis of the third century. Modern scholars debate how far his reign was a period of stability or of mounting weakness.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Potter, The Roman Empire at Bay (2014)

set.detail:
Gnaeus Domitius Annius Ulpianus came from Tyre in Phoenicia, which he proudly calls his patria. He served as assessor to Papinian, perhaps as secretary for petitions (a libellis) under Septimius Severus, and wrote most of his enormous output between about 211 and 217 under Caracalla: 81 books on the praetor's edict, 51 on the civil law of Sabinus, works on the duties of the proconsul (De officio proconsulis, which collected the rescripts against Christians), on adultery, on fideicommissa and many others. Under Elagabalus he may have been exiled; Severus Alexander made him praefectus annonae and then, late in 222, praetorian prefect with extraordinary powers, effectively the leading minister.

Ulpian tried to discipline the Praetorians, who clashed with the people of Rome in three days of street fighting; in 223 (not 228, as a misreading of Dio once suggested) the soldiers attacked him at night and killed him in the palace in the presence of the emperor and his mother. His killer, Epagathus, was removed to Egypt as prefect and later executed.

Ulpian's legacy is immense. Justinian's compilers took about two-fifths of the Digest from his works, more than from any other jurist. Many of the most famous principles of Roman law come from him: justice as 'the constant and perpetual will to render to each his right'; the division of law into public and private, and into natural law, the law of nations and civil law; the claim that by natural law all men are born free and equal; and the statements that 'what pleases the prince has the force of law' and that 'the prince is not bound by the laws', which became central to medieval and early modern theories of sovereignty. Tony Honoré's study reconstructs his career and his ideology of law as a science of justice.

scholarship: Honoré, Ulpian: Pioneer of Human Rights (2nd ed., 2002)

set.detail:
Lucius Cassius Dio was born around 164 at Nicaea in Bithynia, son of the senator Marcus Cassius Apronianus, governor of Cilicia and Dalmatia. He came to Rome around 180, entered the Senate under Commodus, whose performances in the arena he watched from the senatorial seats, and was praetor in 194 or 195 and suffect consul around 205. As a senator he witnessed the murder of Pertinax, the auction of the empire and Severus' entry into Rome, and he accompanied Caracalla to Nicomedia in 214-215. Macrinus appointed him curator of Pergamum and Smyrna. Under Severus Alexander he was proconsul of Africa and legate of Dalmatia and of Pannonia Superior, where his strict discipline made the Praetorians demand his death; nevertheless Alexander made him consul for the second time, as his colleague, in 229, then allowed him to retire to Nicaea because of illness.

Dio began his career as a writer with a pamphlet on the dreams and portents that foretold Severus' rule, which pleased the emperor; that night, he says, a divine sign commanded him to write history. He spent ten years collecting material and twelve writing a Roman History in 80 books from Aeneas to 229. Books 36-60 (69 BC to AD 46) survive largely intact; the rest are known through the eleventh-century epitome of John Xiphilinus, the excerpts of Constantine VII and Zonaras. Written in Attic Greek on the model of Thucydides, it includes set speeches, notably the debate between Agrippa and Maecenas in book 52, which outlines a programme for monarchy that reflects Dio's own Severan concerns.

For the period 180-229 Dio is an eyewitness and the most important source, hostile to Caracalla and suspicious of the soldiers, a senator who believed in good monarchy. Fergus Millar's study (1964) established him as a serious historian.

scholarship: Millar, A Study of Cassius Dio (1964)
Kemezis, Greek Narratives of the Roman Empire under the Severans (2014)

set.detail:
Ardashir, son of Papak and descendant of Sasan, came from a priestly-royal family of Persis (Fars) connected with the temple of Anahita at Istakhr. Around 205-210 his father seized power in Persis as a sub-king of the Parthians; Ardashir, commander of Darabgird, succeeded, eliminating his brother Shapur and local rivals, and expanded into Kerman, Isfahan, Khuzestan and Mesene. He founded the round city of Ardashir-Khwarrah (Gor, modern Firuzabad), with a palace and fire temple. In 224 he defeated and killed the Parthian king Artabanus IV at Hormozgan and around 226 was crowned King of Kings at Ctesiphon, adopting the title 'Mazda-worshipping lord Ardashir, King of Kings of the Iranians, whose lineage is from the gods'.

Ardashir created a more centralised state than the Arsacids, though the great noble families retained much power. His rock reliefs at Naqsh-e Rajab and Naqsh-e Rostam show him receiving the ring of kingship from Ahura Mazda while their horses trample Artabanus and the evil spirit Ahriman; at Firuzabad a vast relief depicts the battle of Hormozgan. Later Sasanian tradition, in the Letter of Tansar and the Testament of Ardashir, made him the founder of a union of throne and Zoroastrian church, and the Middle Persian romance Karnamag-i Ardashir turned his rise into legend.

Ardashir attacked Rome repeatedly. He failed to take Hatra (c. 229), invaded Mesopotamia and besieged Nisibis in 230, faced Severus Alexander's counter-offensive in 232, and in the confusion after 235 captured Nisibis and Carrhae and, with his son Shapur, whom he made co-ruler around 240, finally took Hatra (240-241). Herodian says he claimed all the former Achaemenid lands up to the Aegean; whether this was a real programme is debated. He died around 242, leaving Shapur I an empire ready to challenge Rome.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Wiesehöfer, Ancient Persia (1996)
Daryaee, Sasanian Persia (2009)

set.detail:
Gaius Julius Verus Maximinus, called Thrax (the Thracian), was born around 173 in Thrace or Moesia. The Historia Augusta's tales of a gigantic shepherd over eight feet tall, who could pull carts and crack stones with his hands and was noticed by Septimius Severus at military games, are fiction elaborating Herodian's report that he was of barbarian peasant stock. In reality he was an equestrian officer with a long career, and in 235 was in charge of training recruits from Pannonia at Mogontiacum. When the army turned against Severus Alexander, these recruits proclaimed him, and he became the first emperor to rise from the soldiers and never set foot in Rome.

Maximinus waged a vigorous war across the Rhine in 235-236, sending the Senate paintings of his victories, and the battlefield at the Harzhorn in Lower Saxony, discovered in 2008, shows that his army fought some 200 km beyond the frontier. He then campaigned against the Dacians and Sarmatians from Sirmium (236-237). To pay the army, whose wages he doubled, he resorted to confiscations from the rich and from cities, which Herodian describes in detail, and he persecuted the leaders of the Roman church, exiling Pontian and Hippolytus.

In early 238 a revolt in Africa proclaimed the Gordians, and the Senate declared Maximinus a public enemy. He marched on Italy but was halted by the stubborn defence of Aquileia; his army, short of supplies and worried about their families held at Albanum, mutinied, and soldiers of II Parthica killed him and his son Maximus in their tent in spring 238. Their heads were sent to Rome. The senatorial tradition remembered him as a barbarian tyrant. Modern historians see a competent military emperor whose reign showed the collapse of the bond between Senate and army.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Moosbauer and Berger, "Der Harzhorn-Fund", in Roms vergessener Feldzug (2013)
Börm, "Die Herrschaft des Kaisers Maximinus Thrax", Gymnasium 115 (2008)

set.detail:
Marcus Julius Philippus was born around 204 at Shahba in the Trachonitis, in the province of Arabia, son of a local notable named Julius Marinus. With his brother Gaius Julius Priscus he rose in the equestrian service; Priscus was praetorian prefect under Gordian III, and Philip succeeded Timesitheus in 243. After Gordian's death in the Persian campaign of 244, which Roman sources blame on Philip's intrigues, the army proclaimed him. He made peace with Shapur, paying, according to the Persian inscription, 500,000 denarii, and hurried to Rome, leaving Priscus as 'ruler of the east' (rector Orientis).

Philip raised his son Philip II to Caesar and then Augustus (247) and turned his birthplace into a Roman city, Philippopolis, with a theatre, baths and a temple to his deified father. He fought the Carpi on the Danube (245-247) and in April 248 celebrated Rome's thousandth anniversary with spectacular games; coins show the animals exhibited. In 248-249 revolts broke out: Pacatianus on the Danube, Jotapianus in the east, perhaps Silbannacus. Philip sent the senator Decius to restore order in Moesia; the troops proclaimed Decius, who defeated and killed Philip near Verona in September 249, while the Praetorians killed his son in Rome.

A Christian tradition, reported by Eusebius, says that Philip was a Christian who was made to do penance before attending the Easter vigil at Antioch, and that Origen wrote letters to him and his wife Otacilia Severa. Jerome and later writers called him the first Christian emperor. Most modern scholars doubt it, since his public acts, including the millennial games and the deification of his father, were thoroughly traditional; some suggest sympathy rather than conversion. His Arab origin made him a figure of interest in modern Syrian and Arab historiography.

scholarship: Körner, Philippus Arabs (2002)

set.detail:
Gaius Messius Quintus Decius was born around 201 at Budalia near Sirmium, one of the first of the Danubian emperors, but unlike his successors he was a senator of distinguished career: consul, governor of Moesia Inferior and of Hispania Tarraconensis, and perhaps prefect of Rome. In 248 Philip sent him to restore discipline in the Danube army after the revolt of Pacatianus; the troops proclaimed him in 249, and he defeated Philip near Verona in September. He added the name Traianus, evoking the conqueror of Dacia, and promoted the cult of the deified emperors with a series of coins honouring eleven divi.

Decius' best-known act was the edict of late 249 or early 250 ordering all inhabitants of the empire to sacrifice to the gods and obtain certificates (libelli). Christian writers made him a persecutor, and Lactantius calls him an 'execrable animal'; James Rives has argued that the edict aimed at a collective act of piety for the empire's salvation rather than the destruction of Christianity, though its effect on the church was traumatic. He also built baths on the Aventine and restored the Colosseum after a fire.

Most of his short reign was spent fighting the Goths of Cniva, who invaded in 250. Decius won at Nicopolis but was defeated at Beroe; Philippopolis fell, and its governor Priscus proclaimed himself emperor, while in Rome Valens Licinianus rebelled. In June 251, at Abritus, Decius and his son Herennius Etruscus were killed when the army was trapped in a swamp; his body was never found. He was the first Roman emperor killed by a foreign enemy. His wife Herennia Etruscilla and surviving son Hostilian were left to Trebonianus Gallus, under whom Hostilian died of plague.

scholarship: Rives, "The Decree of Decius and the Religion of Empire", JRS 89 (1999)

set.detail:
Publius Licinius Valerianus, born around 200 into an old Etrurian senatorial family, was a consular by 238, when he appears as an envoy of the Senate in the revolt against Maximinus, and later, according to the Historia Augusta, Decius offered him the revived censorship. In 253 Trebonianus Gallus sent him to bring troops from Raetia and Germany against the usurper Aemilianus; when Gallus was killed, Valerian's army proclaimed him, Aemilianus was murdered by his own soldiers, and Valerian entered Rome in the autumn of 253. He at once made his adult son Gallienus co-Augustus and divided the empire: Gallienus took the west, Valerian the east, where Shapur I had just devastated Syria and sacked Antioch.

Valerian restored Antioch, fought the Goths who raided Asia Minor by sea (256-257), and confronted the Persians, who took Dura-Europos. In 257 and 258 he issued two edicts against the Christians: the first ordered the clergy to sacrifice and banned assemblies and visits to cemeteries, the second ordered the execution of bishops, priests and deacons and the confiscation of the property of Christian senators, equestrians and imperial freedmen. Pope Sixtus II, Lawrence and Cyprian of Carthage were among the victims. Dionysius of Alexandria attributed the persecution to the influence of Valerian's finance minister Macrianus.

In 260, with his army weakened by plague, Valerian marched to relieve Edessa and was captured by Shapur, with his praetorian prefect, senators and soldiers, the only Roman emperor ever taken prisoner by a foreign enemy. He died in captivity at an unknown date. Lactantius' story that Shapur used him as a footstool and later had him flayed is Christian polemic, but Persian reliefs at Naqsh-e Rostam and Bishapur show him as a captive. Gallienus did not attempt to ransom him.

scholarship: Glas, Valerian (2014)

set.detail:
Publius Licinius Egnatius Gallienus was born around 218, son of Valerian and Egnatia Mariniana. Made Augustus by his father in 253, he governed the west while Valerian fought in the east, residing at Cologne and Milan and campaigning against Franks, Alamanni and Juthungi. After Valerian's capture in 260 he ruled alone until 268, facing usurpers in every quarter: Ingenuus and Regalianus on the Danube (260), the Macriani in the east (260-261), Postumus in Gaul (260), Aemilianus in Egypt (261-262) and finally Aureolus in Italy (268). He defeated the Alamanni near Milan (259 or 260) and the Heruli on the Nestus (268), but could not recover Gaul and relied on Odaenathus of Palmyra in the east.

Gallienus' reforms laid foundations for the later recovery. He created a mobile cavalry force based at Milan, from which later emperors such as Aureolus, Claudius and Aurelian emerged; he excluded senators from legionary commands, which went to professional equestrian officers, many of Danubian origin; and he developed the protectores as a corps of officer-cadets. In 260 he issued a rescript ending Valerian's persecution and returning cemeteries and places of worship to the Christians, the first recognition of the church's corporate property. He was a patron of Greek culture: he befriended Plotinus, who asked him to found a city run on Platonic laws in Campania, and was initiated at Eleusis. His portraits revived an idealising, Augustan style.

Gallienus was murdered by his officers during the siege of Milan in 268. The senatorial tradition, resentful of his exclusion of senators and represented by Aurelius Victor and the Historia Augusta, portrayed him as frivolous and effeminate, wearing flowers in his hair and jewels, while the empire collapsed. Lukas de Blois and later scholars reassessed him as a resourceful ruler who held the core of the empire together in its worst crisis.

scholarship: de Blois, The Policy of the Emperor Gallienus (1976)
Geiger, Gallienus (2013)

set.detail:
Shapur, son of Ardashir I, fought beside his father at Hormozgan, where the Firuzabad relief shows him unhorsing an enemy, and was made co-ruler around 240, taking part in the capture of Hatra. Sole King of Kings from about 242 until his death around 270, he expanded his title to 'King of Kings of Iran and non-Iran' (Eran ud Aneran), reflecting conquests that included the Kushan lands in the east and victories over Rome in the west. His great trilingual inscription on the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht at Naqsh-e Rostam (ŠKZ), in Middle Persian, Parthian and Greek, narrates three wars against Rome: the defeat and death of Gordian III at Misiche (244) and the tribute of Philip; the destruction of a Roman army at Barbalissos and the capture of 37 cities including Antioch (252-253); and the capture of Valerian near Edessa (260) and raids into Cilicia and Cappadocia.

Shapur celebrated these victories in rock reliefs at Naqsh-e Rostam, Bishapur and Darabgird, showing the Roman emperors kneeling or held by the hand. He deported tens of thousands of Romans, including skilled craftsmen and Christians, to new cities such as Gundeshapur (Veh-Andiyok-Shabuhr) and Bishapur, where Roman techniques appear in mosaics and buildings; the dam-bridge of Band-e Kaisar at Shushtar is traditionally attributed to Roman prisoners. The inscription also lists fire temples founded for the souls of members of his family and a detailed list of his court.

Shapur showed religious openness: the prophet Mani was received at his court and dedicated to him the Shabuhragan, while the Zoroastrian priest Kartir began his rise. His later years were troubled by Odaenathus' counter-attacks, which reached Ctesiphon in 262 and c. 266. He died around 270 at Bishapur and was succeeded by his son Hormizd I. Shapur was the most successful of all Persian kings against Rome and is the only foreign ruler ever to capture a Roman emperor.

scholarship: Huyse, Die dreisprachige Inschrift Šabuhrs I. an der Ka'ba-i Zardušt (1999)
Canepa, The Two Eyes of the Earth (2009)

set.detail:
Marcus Cassianius Latinius Postumus was a soldier of obscure, probably Gallic or Batavian, origin who by 260 commanded the Rhine frontier under Gallienus. When his troops, quarrelling with Gallienus' son Saloninus and the prefect Silvanus over booty, proclaimed him emperor, he besieged Cologne and had both killed. For nine years he ruled the 'Gallic Empire' (Imperium Galliarum): the Germanies, Gaul, Britain and Spain, and for a time Raetia. His capital was Cologne, later Trier; he appointed consuls, held the consulship himself five times, had a praetorian guard and a senate, and struck a high-quality coinage at Cologne and Lyon, including fine aurei and a famous series of Hercules' labours, with titles such as Restitutor Galliarum and Germanicus Maximus.

Postumus presented himself as the defender of the west against the Franks and Alamanni, and his reign brought relative security to Gaul. He did not march on Rome or claim the whole empire. Gallienus attacked him around 265, won a victory but was wounded by an arrow during the siege of a Gallic city, and gave up. In 268 Aureolus at Milan may have declared for Postumus, who did not come to his aid.

In 269 Ulpius Cornelius Laelianus rebelled at Mogontiacum. Postumus took the city but refused to let his soldiers sack it, and they murdered him. He was succeeded briefly by Marius and then Victorinus, and the Spanish provinces returned to Claudius II. The Gallic Empire survived until 274. John Drinkwater's study established the now dominant view that Postumus was not a separatist or Gallic nationalist but a Roman emperor whose ambitions were limited by circumstances, responding to the west's need for an emperor present on the frontier.

scholarship: Drinkwater, The Gallic Empire (1987)

set.detail:
Septimius Odaenathus was born around 220 into one of the leading families of Palmyra, the caravan city between Syria and the Euphrates; his family had received Roman citizenship from Septimius Severus, and his father Hairan held the title exarch (ras) of the Palmyrenes. By the 250s Odaenathus was a senator of consular rank and lord of Tadmor. Petrus Patricius tells that before 260 he sent gifts to Shapur I, who contemptuously had them thrown into the Euphrates, demanding that he come in person as a suppliant.

After Valerian's capture in 260, Odaenathus attacked Shapur's retreating army on the Euphrates and then, in 261, crushed the usurper Quietus at Emesa on behalf of Gallienus, who rewarded him with an extraordinary command over the east as dux Romanorum and corrector totius Orientis. He reorganised the remnants of the Roman eastern army together with Palmyrene heavy cavalry and archers. In 262 he recovered Carrhae and Nisibis and advanced to Ctesiphon, and he returned there around 266-267. He assumed the Iranian title King of Kings, crowning his eldest son Herodes as co-ruler, and inscriptions in Palmyra honour him as 'king of kings and restorer of the whole east'.

Around 267-268 he went to Asia Minor to fight Gothic raiders, and he was murdered with Herodes, at Emesa or at Heraclea Pontica, by a relative named Maeonius, perhaps over a personal quarrel; ancient writers suspected Zenobia or Gallienus. His widow Zenobia took power for their son Vaballathus and built on his position to create the short-lived Palmyrene empire. Historians debate whether Odaenathus was essentially a loyal Roman official and client of Gallienus, as Zosimus and Festus imply, or an independent dynast, but agree that he saved the Roman east in its darkest years.

scholarship: Hartmann, Das palmyrenische Teilreich (2001)
Andrade, Zenobia (2018)

set.detail:
Septimia Zenobia, in Aramaic Bat-Zabbai, was born around 240 into a Palmyrene family and became the second wife of Odaenathus, bearing him Vaballathus and possibly other sons. Ancient and modern legend made her a figure of exceptional beauty, learning and chastity: the Historia Augusta claims she spoke Egyptian, Greek and Aramaic, wrote a history of the east, hunted, drank with her generals and claimed descent from Cleopatra and Dido, much of which is invention. She surrounded herself with Greek intellectuals, including the philosopher and critic Cassius Longinus, and an inscription from Egypt honouring a synagogue by order of 'the queen and the king' may refer to her and Vaballathus.

After Odaenathus' murder in 267 or 268 she ruled in the name of Vaballathus, who inherited his father's titles. In 270, after Claudius II's death, her general Zabdas conquered Egypt and Arabia and her armies advanced through Asia Minor to Ancyra and Chalcedon. At first Palmyrene coins and documents recognised Aurelian as Augustus, with Vaballathus as king, imperator and dux Romanorum; in 272 Vaballathus became Augustus and Zenobia Augusta. Aurelian invaded, defeated Zabdas at Immae and Emesa, and besieged Palmyra; Zenobia fled towards Persia on a camel but was captured at the Euphrates.

At her trial in Emesa she blamed her advisers, and Longinus was executed. Zosimus says she died on the way to Rome, but the Latin tradition says she walked in Aurelian's triumph in 274, loaded with golden chains so heavy that a jester had to support them, and then lived on a villa near Tibur, marrying into the Roman aristocracy. Her afterlife is rich: Boccaccio, Chaucer and Orientalist painters celebrated her, and in modern Syria she became a national symbol, appearing on banknotes. Andrade's biography stresses her as a regent operating within Roman structures.

scholarship: Andrade, Zenobia: Shooting Star of Palmyra (2018)
Southern, Empress Zenobia: Palmyra's Rebel Queen (2008)

set.detail:
Lucius Domitius Aurelianus was born on 9 September 214 or 215, probably near Sirmium or in Moesia, of humble family. A cavalry officer of exceptional toughness, nicknamed 'manu ad ferrum' (hand on the sword), he served under Gallienus and commanded the cavalry under Claudius II in the Gothic war. On Claudius' death in 270 the army proclaimed him at Sirmium, and Claudius' brother Quintillus, recognised in Italy, died within weeks. In five years Aurelian reunited the empire. He defeated Juthungi and Vandals, suffered a defeat near Placentia before winning at Fanum Fortunae and Ticinum (271), crushed a revolt of the Rome mint workers, began the Aurelian Walls, defeated the Goths beyond the Danube and abandoned Trajan's Dacia. In 272 he conquered the Palmyrene empire, capturing Zenobia, and sacked Palmyra after its second revolt in 273; in 274 he defeated Tetricus at Châlons and celebrated a magnificent triumph as Restitutor Orbis.

Aurelian reorganised the coinage, introducing a radiate with a fixed silver content marked XXI, reformed the Roman food dole to provide daily bread, pork, oil and salt, and established the cult of Sol Invictus as the empire's supreme deity, building a great temple in the Campus Agrippae, dedicated on 25 December 274, with a new college of pontiffs. Coins of Serdica style him 'deus et dominus natus', god and lord by birth, a step towards the autocracy of the later empire. His discipline was severe.

In autumn 275, on his way to a Persian war, he was murdered near Caenophrurium in Thrace by officers persuaded by his secretary Eros, threatened with punishment, that their names were on a death list. The Senate deified him. The Historia Augusta's story of a six-month interregnum is false. His wife Ulpia Severina may have governed briefly; Alaric Watson's study presents Aurelian as the architect of the third-century recovery.

scholarship: Watson, Aurelian and the Third Century (1999)

set.detail:
Marcus Aurelius Probus was born at Sirmium on 19 August 232 and rose as an officer under Valerian, Gallienus, Claudius II and Aurelian; the Historia Augusta's life of him is largely invented, and he is often confused with Tenagino Probus, prefect of Egypt in 270. In 276, commanding in the east, he was proclaimed emperor by his troops against Florianus, who had succeeded his half-brother Tacitus; Florianus' army, bogged down near Tarsus in the summer heat, killed him.

Probus spent his reign campaigning. In 277-278 he cleared Gaul of Franks and Alamanni who had sacked many cities after 275, recovering according to the Historia Augusta sixty of them, and pushed the invaders back across the Rhine; he defeated Burgundians and Vandals in Raetia and sent captives to Britain. His generals suppressed the Isaurian bandit Lydius at Cremna and drove the Blemmyes from Upper Egypt. He settled large numbers of barbarians in the empire, including 100,000 Bastarnae in Thrace, while Franks settled on the Black Sea coast escaped on an astonishing voyage that took them back to the Rhine via Sicily and Gibraltar. He crushed the usurpers Saturninus in the east and Proculus and Bonosus in Gaul (280-281). He also permitted vine growing in Gaul, Spain, Britain and Pannonia and used soldiers to plant vineyards and drain marshes, celebrating a triumph in Rome in 281.

In 282, while his soldiers were draining marshland at Sirmium, they mutinied and killed him in an iron watchtower, perhaps after news that the praetorian prefect Carus had been proclaimed in Raetia; the story that he had boasted that soon the empire would need no soldiers is probably a later justification. His coinage is notable for an exceptional variety of bust types and legends, making it a favourite field for collectors.

scholarship: Kreucher, Der Kaiser Marcus Aurelius Probus und seine Zeit (2003)

set.detail:
Diocles was born around 244, probably near Salona in Dalmatia, of humble origins: Aurelius Victor and the Epitome say he was the son of a scribe or a freedman of a senator. He served as an officer, possibly as dux of Moesia, and by 284 commanded the imperial bodyguard (protectores domestici). After Numerian's death the army proclaimed him on 20 November 284 at Nicomedia, and he killed the prefect Aper with his own hand. He took the name Gaius Aurelius Valerius Diocletianus, defeated Carinus in 285, and in 285-286 made Maximian first Caesar and then Augustus. In 293 he created the Tetrarchy with Constantius and Galerius as Caesars.

Diocletian's reign of twenty years transformed the Roman state. He roughly doubled the number of provinces and grouped them in dioceses, separated civil and military authority, enlarged the army and built forts on all frontiers, including the Strata Diocletiana, introduced a census-based tax system with the indiction, reformed the coinage (294) and issued the Edict on Maximum Prices (301). The Gregorian and Hermogenian codes collected imperial rescripts. He elevated the ceremony of the court, wearing jewelled robes and requiring adoratio (prostration), and advertised the rulers' divine protection by Jupiter and Hercules. His wars restored the frontiers: Carausius and Allectus were defeated in Britain (296), Egypt was reconquered (297-298) and Galerius' victory over Narseh (298) brought the favourable Peace of Nisibis.

In 303 he launched the Great Persecution of the Christians, apparently under Galerius' influence. After a severe illness he abdicated at Nicomedia on 1 May 305 and retired to his palace at Split, refusing in 308 to return to power. He saw his system collapse into civil war, his statues pulled down and his wife Prisca and daughter Valeria executed by Licinius, and died, perhaps by starvation, around 311-312. Lactantius damns him; modern historians (Barnes, Kolb, Leadbetter) see him as the founder of the late Roman state.

scholarship: Barnes, The New Empire of Diocletian and Constantine (1982)
Kolb, Diocletian und die Erste Tetrarchie (1987)
Roberto, Diocleziano (2014)

set.detail:
Marcus Aurelius Valerius Maximianus was born around 250 near Sirmium to a family of shopkeepers; Aurelius Victor calls him half-civilised. A capable soldier, he served under Aurelian and Probus and was a long-standing comrade of Diocletian, who made him Caesar in 285 and Augustus in 286. As Herculius, protected by Hercules, he ruled the west from Milan and Trier while Diocletian, Jovius, held the senior position. He crushed the Bagaudae in Gaul (285-286), fought Alamanni, Burgundians, Heruli and Franks, crossed the Rhine in 287 and made the Frankish king Gennobaudes a client, but lost Britain to Carausius and failed in a naval expedition against him (289). In 296-298 he campaigned in Spain and Mauretania against the Quinquegentiani and entered Carthage in triumph. He enforced the persecution of 303-305 harshly in Italy and Africa.

Maximian abdicated reluctantly on 1 May 305 at Milan, alongside Diocletian, and retired to Lucania. When his son Maxentius was proclaimed at Rome in 306, Maximian resumed the purple, helped defeat Severus, and in 307 married his daughter Fausta to Constantine at Trier, granting him the title Augustus. In April 308 he tried to depose Maxentius before the troops in Rome, failed, and fled to Constantine. At the conference of Carnuntum in November 308 he was forced to abdicate again.

In 310, while Constantine was on the Rhine, Maximian proclaimed himself emperor again at Arles, seized the treasury and fled to Massilia when Constantine returned. Captured, he died, officially by suicide, by hanging; Lactantius adds a story that he tried to murder Constantine in his bed and killed a eunuch placed there instead. His memory was condemned, but after 318 Constantine rehabilitated him as divus, ancestor of his sons through Fausta. Lactantius portrays him as violent and lustful.

scholarship: Barnes, The New Empire of Diocletian and Constantine (1982)

set.detail:
Flavius Valerius Constantius, called in later Byzantine sources Chlorus ('the pale'), was born around 250 in the Balkans, of modest Illyrian family; the claim of descent from Claudius II was invented by Constantine's propagandists in 310. A protector and tribune, perhaps governor of Dalmatia, he formed a union with Helena, a woman of low birth, whether marriage or concubinage is disputed, and their son Constantine was born at Naissus around 272-273. Around 289 he married Theodora, Maximian's stepdaughter, with whom he had six children, including Julius Constantius (Julian's father), Flavius Dalmatius and Constantia, Licinius' future wife. As Maximian's praetorian prefect, he was appointed Caesar on 1 March 293.

Constantius' main task was the recovery of Britain from Carausius and Allectus. In 293 he took Gesoriacum after blocking its harbour with a mole, then cleared the Rhine delta of the usurpers' Frankish allies and settled captives in Gaul. In 296 his fleet crossed in two divisions; his prefect Asclepiodotus defeated and killed Allectus, and Constantius entered London, celebrated on the Arras medallion as 'restorer of the eternal light'. He then defeated the Alamanni at Lingones and Vindonissa (298) and made Trier his capital, rebuilding the city and its defences. During the Great Persecution, according to Lactantius, he merely demolished churches; Eusebius says he did not harm Christians at all, and the Donatists later asked the Gallic church to judge their case because it had no traditores.

On 1 May 305 Constantius became senior Augustus. He summoned Constantine from Galerius' court and campaigned with him against the Picts beyond Hadrian's Wall. He died at Eboracum on 25 July 306, and his army proclaimed his son. Later Christian writers presented him as a crypto-monotheist; panegyrists praised his clemency and moderation.

scholarship: Barnes, Constantine (2011)
Casey, Carausius and Allectus (1994)

set.detail:
Gaius Galerius Valerius Maximianus was born around 258-260 near Serdica in Dacia Ripensis, to a peasant family; his mother Romula, he claimed, came from across the Danube, and he was nicknamed Armentarius, the herdsman. Lactantius depicts him as a huge, savage man, contemptuous of Romans and fond of feeding men to bears. A career soldier, he was made Caesar by Diocletian on 1 March 293 and married Diocletian's daughter Valeria. In 293-294 he suppressed unrest in Egypt; from 295 he fought the Carpi on the lower Danube, resettling them in Pannonia; in 296-297 he was defeated by the Persians near Callinicum, but in 298 he won the decisive victory over Narseh in Armenia, capturing the royal harem and treasure. His palace, arch and rotunda at Thessalonica celebrate these victories.

Lactantius blames Galerius for instigating the Great Persecution of 303 and for pressuring Diocletian to abdicate in 305 and appoint Galerius' protégés Severus and Maximinus Daia as Caesars. As senior Augustus from 306 he failed to control the dynastic revolts: he recognised Constantine only as Caesar, lost Severus to Maxentius and failed in his own invasion of Italy (307), whose size he found unexpectedly daunting. At the conference of Carnuntum (308) he made his old friend Licinius Augustus. He drained Lake Pelso (Balaton) and created the province of Valeria, named after his wife, and built the palace of Felix Romuliana at his birthplace.

Dying of a horrible disease, probably cancer, he issued the edict of toleration at Serdica on 30 April 311, granting Christians the right to exist and worship, and died days later; he was buried at Romuliana. Bill Leadbetter's study presents him as a capable soldier and the true heir of Diocletian's vision, distorted by Lactantius' polemic.

scholarship: Leadbetter, Galerius and the Will of Diocletian (2009)

set.detail:
Marcus Aurelius Valerius Maxentius was born around 278-283, son of Maximian and his Syrian wife Eutropia, and married Galerius' daughter Valeria Maximilla, by whom he had a son, Valerius Romulus. Excluded from the succession in 305, he lived as a private citizen near Rome until 28 October 306, when the Praetorians and people, angry at Galerius' plans to tax the city and abolish the Guard, proclaimed him princeps. He took the title Augustus in 307, defeated the invasions of Severus and Galerius with the help of his father's prestige, and survived his father's attempt to depose him in 308. Africa revolted under Domitius Alexander in 308, causing famine in Rome, until his prefect Volusianus recovered it in 309-310.

Maxentius styled himself 'conservator urbis suae', preserver of his city, and was the last emperor to reside in Rome for long. His building programme was vast: the Basilica Nova on the Velia, completed by Constantine, the restoration of the Temple of Venus and Roma after a fire, the raising of the Aurelian Walls, and a villa, circus and dynastic mausoleum on the Via Appia, where his son, who died in 309, was buried and deified. He ended the persecution in his territories, restored property to the church and tolerated the election of bishops in Rome, though he exiled the rival bishops Marcellus and Eusebius after riots.

After Maximian's death in 310, Maxentius proclaimed himself his avenger and declared war on Constantine, who invaded Italy in 312. Maxentius was defeated and drowned in the Tiber at the Milvian Bridge on 28 October 312. Constantinian propaganda made him a tyrant, oppressive and debauched. In 2006 excavators on the Palatine found imperial sceptres and standards hidden in a pit, plausibly buried by his supporters after his defeat.

scholarship: Cullhed, Conservator Urbis Suae (1994)
Panella (ed.), I segni del potere: realtà e immaginario della sovranità nella Roma imperiale (2011)

set.detail:
Valerius Licinianus Licinius was born around 265 in Moesia or Dacia, of peasant stock, and was an old friend and comrade of Galerius, with whom he served in the Persian war. At the conference of Carnuntum on 11 November 308 Galerius made him Augustus directly, without his having been Caesar, with responsibility for Illyricum. After Galerius' death in 311 he occupied the Balkans, and in February 313 he met Constantine at Milan, married his half-sister Constantia and agreed on religious toleration and restitution of property to the church. Maximinus Daia invaded his territory, but Licinius defeated him at Tzirallum (Campus Ergenus) on 30 April 313, after his soldiers, according to Lactantius, recited a monotheistic prayer revealed to Licinius by an angel. Licinius then published the Milan agreement at Nicomedia and executed the families of Galerius, Severus, Maximinus and Diocletian, including Prisca and Valeria.

The alliance with Constantine soon broke down. In the first civil war, dated 316 by most scholars (some prefer 314), Licinius was defeated at Cibalae and Mardia and ceded all the Balkans except Thrace; in 317 their sons Crispus, Constantine II and Licinius II were made Caesars. Tensions grew in the early 320s: Licinius restricted the church in his territories, banning synods and expelling Christians from his court, and Constantine pursued Sarmatians and Goths into Licinius' lands.

In 324 Constantine defeated Licinius at Adrianople, the Hellespont and Chrysopolis. Licinius surrendered at Nicomedia on the promise of his life, at Constantia's plea, but was executed at Thessalonica in 325, charged with plotting; his son was executed in 326. Eusebius made him a persecutor and enemy of God; the Epitome says he despised learning, calling it a poison and a public pest. Modern historians see him as a competent soldier ruler destroyed by a more ambitious colleague.

scholarship: Barnes, Constantine (2011)

set.detail:
Flavius Valerius Constantinus was born at Naissus on 27 February around 272-273, son of Constantius and Helena. He grew up at the courts of Diocletian and Galerius, fought in the east and on the Danube, and witnessed the beginning of the persecution at Nicomedia in 303. Passed over in 305, he joined his father in Britain and was proclaimed Augustus at York on 25 July 306. From Trier he defended the Rhine against the Franks, married Maximian's daughter Fausta (307) and eliminated his father-in-law (310). In 312 he invaded Italy and defeated Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge after the vision or dream that made the Christian sign his standard. Allied with Licinius by the Milan agreement of 313, he fought him in 316 and again in 324, becoming sole emperor after Chrysopolis.

Constantine's rule transformed the empire. He favoured the church with buildings (the Lateran, St Peter's, the Holy Sepulchre), legal privileges for the clergy, episcopal courts and the Sunday holiday, and intervened in church disputes, from the Donatists to the Arians, convening the Council of Nicaea in 325. He founded Constantinople (324-330) as a new imperial city. He introduced the gold solidus, completed the separation of civil and military command, created the field army and the magistri militum, and issued laws on family, slaves and coloni. His wars against the Goths (332) and Sarmatians (334) secured the Danube, and he planned a Persian war when he died.

In 326 he had his eldest son Crispus executed at Pola and his wife Fausta killed, in circumstances still unexplained. He was baptised on his deathbed by Eusebius of Nicomedia and died near Nicomedia on 22 May 337. Eusebius' Life presents him as God's chosen ruler; Julian and Zosimus as a spendthrift innovator. The debate on the nature and timing of his conversion and his aims continues (Barnes, Bleckmann, Van Dam, Potter).

scholarship: Barnes, Constantine: Dynasty, Religion and Power in the Later Roman Empire (2011)
Lenski (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to the Age of Constantine (2006)
Potter, Constantine the Emperor (2013)

set.detail:
Flavia Julia Helena was born around 248, probably at Drepanum in Bithynia, which Constantine later renamed Helenopolis. Ambrose calls her a stabularia, a stable-girl or innkeeper's servant, and the Origo and other sources imply low birth. Whether she was the legal wife or the concubine of Constantius is disputed; she bore him Constantine at Naissus around 272-273 and was set aside around 289 when Constantius married Theodora. Little is known of her life until her son's rise: she may have lived at Trier, where later tradition claimed her palace became the cathedral, and from 312 she resided in Rome, in the Sessorian palace, which included the baths later called Thermae Helenianae and a hall converted into the church of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.

Constantine named her nobilissima femina and in 324 Augusta, and coins were struck in her name. Eusebius says that through her son she became a devout Christian. After the deaths of Crispus and Fausta in 326, in which she may have played a part (Zosimus says she was grief-stricken at Crispus' death), she made a journey through the eastern provinces to Palestine, praying at the holy places, distributing gifts to soldiers, the poor and cities, and founding churches at Bethlehem and on the Mount of Olives, while Constantine built the church of the Holy Sepulchre.

She died around 329 aged about eighty, probably in Constantine's presence, and was buried in the mausoleum on the Via Labicana, in a massive porphyry sarcophagus decorated with cavalry battles, now in the Vatican Museums. From the late fourth century, beginning with Ambrose in 395, she was credited with finding the True Cross in Jerusalem, a legend that made her one of the most venerated saints of the Middle Ages and patron of archaeologists. Jan Willem Drijvers separated the history from the legend.

scholarship: Drijvers, Helena Augusta (1992)
Harbus, Helena of Britain in Medieval Legend (2002)

set.detail:
Flavius Julius Constantius, born at Sirmium on 7 August 317, was the second son of Constantine and Fausta. Caesar from 8 November 324, he was given the east in 335 and became Augustus in September 337 after the massacre of his relatives, which many contemporaries attributed to him. For thirteen years he fought Shapur II on the Mesopotamian frontier, with nine major engagements according to Festus, including the night battle at Singara and three sieges of Nisibis, all repulsed. After the murder of Constans (350) he defeated Magnentius at Mursa (351) and Mons Seleucus (353), becoming sole emperor. He appointed his cousins Gallus (351-354), whom he executed, and Julian (355) as Caesars.

Constantius was a conscientious ruler, devoted to administration and court ceremonial; Ammianus describes his entry into Rome in 357, standing motionless in his chariot like a statue, ducking his head under high gateways though he was short. He visited the city's monuments with admiration and set up an obelisk in the Circus Maximus, while removing the Altar of Victory from the Senate house. He enlarged the senate of Constantinople, recruiting through Themistius, and dedicated the first Hagia Sophia. In religion he favoured a Homoian compromise, summoning councils at Arles, Milan, Sirmium, Rimini and Seleucia and exiling Athanasius, Liberius, Hilary and others who resisted. He issued laws closing temples and banning sacrifice.

In 359-360 he went east against Shapur, who had taken Amida, Singara and Bezabde. When Julian was proclaimed Augustus in Gaul, Constantius prepared to march west but died of fever at Mopsucrenae in Cilicia on 3 November 361, after baptism, naming Julian his heir. Ammianus and Julian portray him as suspicious, cruel and ruled by eunuchs; Athanasius as a persecutor. Recent historians (Barnes, Henck) offer a more balanced assessment.

scholarship: Barnes, Athanasius and Constantius (1993)
Baker-Brian and Tougher (eds), The Sons of Constantine (2020)

set.detail:
Flavius Claudius Julianus was born in Constantinople in 331 or 332, son of Constantine's half-brother Julius Constantius and Basilina. In the massacre of 337 his father and most male relatives were killed; Julian, aged six, and his half-brother Gallus were spared. Educated by the eunuch Mardonius, who taught him Homer, and later kept with Gallus on the remote imperial estate of Macellum in Cappadocia (c. 342-348), he was raised as a Christian and served as a lector. As a student at Nicomedia, Pergamum and Ephesus he studied the works of Libanius and met the Neoplatonist Maximus of Ephesus, and around 351 he secretly turned to the gods. In 355 he studied at Athens, where he met Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus.

On 6 November 355 Constantius made him Caesar, married him to his sister Helena and sent him to Gaul. Against expectations Julian proved a gifted commander: he defeated the Alamanni at Argentoratum (357), subdued the Franks, crossed the Rhine three times and reformed Gallic taxation. Proclaimed Augustus by his troops at Paris in 360, he marched east and became sole emperor on Constantius' death in November 361. In twenty months he purged the palace, tried the old regime's ministers at Chalcedon, cut taxes and court expenses, restored city councils, reopened the temples and tried to create a pagan church, excluded Christians from teaching the classics and planned to rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem. At Antioch, quarrelling with the citizens, he wrote the Misopogon. His writings include orations, hymns to Helios and the Mother of the Gods, the satire The Caesars, Against the Galilaeans and many letters.

In March 363 he invaded Persia, reached Ctesiphon but could not take it, burned his fleet and retreated; he was mortally wounded on 26 June 363. Ammianus admired him with reservations; Christians called him the Apostate.

scholarship: Bowersock, Julian the Apostate (1978)
Tougher, Julian the Apostate (2007)
Elm, Sons of Hellenism, Fathers of the Church (2012)

set.detail:
Shapur II, son of Hormizd II, was born in 309 and, according to Persian tradition preserved by al-Tabari, crowned while still in his mother's womb by the nobles placing the crown on her belly. He reigned for seventy years, until 379, the longest reign of any Sasanian king. As a young man he punished Arab raiders who had attacked Persia during his minority, crossing into Arabia and reputedly piercing the shoulders of captives, which earned him the Arabic epithet Dhu al-Aktaf, 'he of the shoulders'.

Shapur rejected the Peace of Nisibis of 299 and from 337 fought a long war against Constantius II. He besieged Nisibis three times (338, 346, 350), the last time flooding the plain with the river Mygdonius, without success; he won the night battle at Singara but could not break the Roman fortress line. After war against the Chionites and other nomads in the east, he returned in 359 with Chionite allies, sending Constantius a letter claiming all lands to the Strymon, and took Amida after 73 days, followed by Singara and Bezabde (360). In 363 he defeated Julian's invasion by scorched earth and harassment and obtained from Jovian the cession of Nisibis, Singara and the Transtigritane regions and the abandonment of Armenia. He then captured the Armenian king Arsaces II, besieged Artogerassa and fought Valens' generals over Armenia and Iberia until a truce in the late 370s.

From about 340 Shapur persecuted the Christians of his empire, whom he saw as allies of the Christian Roman emperor, imposing a double tax and executing bishop Simeon bar Sabbae of Seleucia-Ctesiphon in 344 or 345 with many clergy; Syriac acts of the Persian martyrs describe the persecution. He also founded cities, including Eranshahr-Shabuhr (Susa rebuilt). He died in 379, leaving Persia at the height of its power.

scholarship: Daryaee, Sasanian Persia (2009)
Dignas and Winter, Rome and Persia in Late Antiquity (2007)

set.detail:
Flavius Valentinianus was born in 321 at Cibalae in Pannonia, son of Gratian the Elder, a Pannonian of humble origins nicknamed Funarius (the rope-maker) who rose to command in Africa and Britain. Valentinian served as an officer in Gaul under Constantius and Julian, was dismissed after a dispute in 357, and is said by Christian writers to have been exiled by Julian for his faith, though this is doubtful. He was tribune of a guard regiment when the officers at Nicaea chose him as emperor on 26 February 364. He made his brother Valens co-Augustus and took the west, living at Milan and from 367 at Trier.

Valentinian was a soldier emperor of great energy and violent temper. He fought the Alamanni for most of his reign (Solicinium, 368), fortified the Rhine and Danube with new forts, burgi and bridgeheads, and sent Count Theodosius to restore Britain after the 'barbarian conspiracy' of 367 and to suppress the revolt of Firmus in Africa (372-375). He created the office of defensor civitatis to protect the poor, legislated on education and medicine in Rome, and kept religious neutrality: Ammianus praises him for leaving everyone free to worship as they wished, though he was a Nicene Christian. His harshness was legendary: Ammianus reports he kept two man-eating bears near his bedroom, named Innocence and Gold-dust, and allowed his prefect Maximinus to conduct treason and magic trials against the Roman aristocracy.

In 367 he made his eight-year-old son Gratian Augustus. He married a second wife, Justina, mother of Valentinian II. In 375, receiving envoys of the Quadi at Brigetio after their invasion of Pannonia, he flew into a rage and died of a stroke on 17 November. Ammianus' portrait, balanced between admiration and horror, is the basis of all later judgements.

scholarship: Lenski, Failure of Empire (2002)
Drinkwater, The Alamanni and Rome (2007)

set.detail:
Flavius Valens was born in 328 at Cibalae, younger brother of Valentinian I, and had an undistinguished career as a guards officer before his brother made him co-Augustus on 28 March 364 and gave him the east. Almost at once he faced the revolt of Procopius, a relative of Julian, who seized Constantinople in September 365; Valens nearly abdicated but defeated him at Thyatira and Nacolia in 366 with the help of veteran generals. He then fought the Goths of Athanaric for their support of Procopius (367-369), concluding peace in a meeting on boats in the middle of the Danube, since Athanaric had sworn never to set foot on Roman soil. In the east he contested Armenia and Iberia with Shapur II, supporting King Pap and then having him murdered (374-375).

Valens was a careful administrator who cut taxes, notably the aurum coronarium, and completed the great aqueduct of Constantinople that still bears his name. From 371 he resided at Antioch, where magic and treason trials, provoked by a seance that spelled out the letters THEOD as the name of his successor, led to many executions. A Homoian Christian, he exiled Nicene bishops, clashed with Basil of Caesarea and conscripted monks; Nicene writers made him a persecutor.

In 376 he allowed the Tervingi, fleeing the Huns, to cross the Danube, hoping for recruits. Mismanagement and exploitation by his officials provoked their revolt, and in 378 he returned from the east to fight them. Unwilling to wait for Gratian, he attacked the Gothic camp near Adrianople on 9 August 378 and was killed with two-thirds of his army; his body was never found. Ammianus calls him uneducated, timid and cruel; Noel Lenski's study portrays a ruler doing his best in an impossible strategic position.

scholarship: Lenski, Failure of Empire: Valens and the Roman State in the Fourth Century AD (2002)

set.detail:
Flavius Gratianus was born at Sirmium on 18 April 359, son of Valentinian I and his first wife Marina Severa. Consul as a child in 366, he was proclaimed Augustus by his father at Ambiani (Amiens) on 24 August 367, aged eight, and educated by the poet Ausonius, who rose with him to the consulship. In 374 he married Constantia, the posthumous daughter of Constantius II, linking his house to the Constantinian dynasty. On his father's death in 375 he became senior Augustus in the west, though the generals proclaimed his half-brother Valentinian II without consulting him.

In 378 Gratian defeated the Lentienses at Argentaria and crossed the Rhine, then marched east to help Valens, but arrived too late for Adrianople. Responsible for the whole empire, he appointed Theodosius as Augustus of the east in January 379 and settled the Greuthungi of Alatheus and Saphrax in Pannonia. He moved his court to Milan around 381, falling under the influence of Ambrose, who wrote De Fide for him. In 382 he removed the Altar of Victory from the Senate house, confiscated the endowments of the Vestals and pagan priesthoods and, according to Zosimus, refused the title and robe of pontifex maximus, though the date and even the historicity of the last are debated.

Gratian was devoted to hunting and archery and surrounded himself with an Alan bodyguard whose dress he adopted, which alienated the regular army. In 383 the British army proclaimed Magnus Maximus. When Maximus crossed to Gaul, Gratian's troops deserted near Paris; he fled and was killed at Lugdunum by Maximus' general Andragathius on 25 August 383, aged 24. Ammianus thought he might have rivalled the best emperors had he not been diverted by frivolous pursuits; Ambrose mourned him as a pious Christian ruler.

scholarship: McLynn, Ambrose of Milan (1994)
Cameron, The Last Pagans of Rome (2011)

Flavius Theodosius was born on 11 January 347 at Cauca in Gallaecia, son of the general Count Theodosius. He served with his father in Britain and Africa and as dux of Moesia Prima defeated the Sarmatians in 374. After his father's execution in 376 he retired to Spain; after Adrianople Gratian recalled him and made him Augustus of the east on 19 January 379. He rebuilt the eastern army, fought the Goths from Thessalonica and in 382 concluded the treaty that settled them in Thrace as a people under their own leaders, obliged to fight for Rome. Baptised during an illness in 380, he issued the edict of Thessalonica defining orthodoxy, expelled the Homoian clergy from Constantinople and summoned the council of 381.

Theodosius recognised Magnus Maximus after Gratian's murder (383) but defeated him in 388 at Siscia and Poetovio after Maximus invaded Italy; he married Galla, sister of Valentinian II. He visited Rome in 389. In 390 he ordered the massacre of Thessalonica and performed public penance at Ambrose's demand. His laws of 391-392 banned sacrifice and temple visits and finally all pagan cult, even in private, and the Serapeum of Alexandria was destroyed. After Valentinian II's death in 392 and the proclamation of Eugenius by Arbogast, he defeated them at the Frigidus in September 394, becoming sole ruler of the whole empire for a few months.

He died at Milan on 17 January 395, leaving the east to Arcadius and the west to Honorius under Stilicho; Ambrose delivered the funeral oration. His monuments include the obelisk in the Hippodrome of Constantinople, the Forum of Theodosius and the silver Missorium of his decennalia (388) now in Madrid. Christian writers called him 'the Great'; Zosimus blamed his extravagance and the barbarisation of the army for Rome's fall.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

scholarship: Williams and Friell, Theodosius: The Empire at Bay (1994)
Errington, Roman Imperial Policy from Julian to Theodosius (2006)
Leppin, Theodosius der Grosse (2003)

Aurelius Ambrosius was born around 339 at Trier, where his father was praetorian prefect of the Gauls. After his father's death the family moved to Rome, where Ambrose received an aristocratic education and became an advocate. Sextus Petronius Probus appointed him consularis of Aemilia and Liguria at Milan around 370. When the Homoian bishop Auxentius died in 374, Ambrose, as governor, went to the church to keep order during the disputed election, and the crowd, prompted, Paulinus says, by a child's cry, acclaimed him bishop. Though only a catechumen, he was baptised and consecrated within a week, on 7 December 374, and gave away his property.

Ambrose became the most powerful churchman of the west. He studied Greek theology, especially Basil and Origen, and wrote on ethics (De officiis ministrorum, modelled on Cicero), on faith and the Holy Spirit for Gratian, on the six days of creation and on virginity, and composed hymns in iambic dimeters that founded the tradition of Latin hymnody. He presided over the council of Aquileia (381), defeated Symmachus' plea for the Altar of Victory (384), and in 385-386 resisted the empress Justina's demand for a basilica for the Homoians by occupying it with his congregation, singing hymns; during the conflict he discovered the relics of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. He forced Theodosius to cancel the restoration of a synagogue burned at Callinicum (388) and imposed penance after the massacre of Thessalonica (390). He baptised Augustine at Easter 387.

Ambrose died on 4 April 397. His secretary Paulinus wrote his Life. Neil McLynn's study portrays him as a supremely skilful politician who used the church to build power in a Christian capital, more than the heroic champion of church independence of later legend.

scholarship: McLynn, Ambrose of Milan: Church and Court in a Christian Capital (1994)
Liebeschuetz, Ambrose of Milan: Political Letters and Speeches (2005)

Athanasius was born in Alexandria around 295-299 and was brought up in the household of Bishop Alexander, whom he served as deacon and secretary at Nicaea. Consecrated bishop on 8 June 328 at about thirty, he ruled the see for 45 years, of which 17 were spent in five exiles. Accused by the Melitians and the supporters of Eusebius of Nicomedia of violence, of breaking a chalice, of murdering the Melitian bishop Arsenius (who was produced alive with both hands) and of threatening the grain supply, he was condemned at Tyre (335) and exiled by Constantine to Trier. Restored in 337, he fled to Rome in 339, returned in 346, escaped a military assault on his church in 356 and spent six years hidden among the Egyptian monks, was exiled again by Julian (362-363) and briefly by Valens (365-366), dying in office on 2 May 373.

Athanasius made himself the champion of the Nicene creed and the homoousios, and his writings created the image of an 'Arian' conspiracy against orthodoxy that dominated later historiography. His works include the double treatise Against the Pagans and On the Incarnation, the Orations against the Arians, the defensive and historical Apologies, the History of the Arians, De Synodis and the Life of Antony (c. 357), which popularised monasticism across the Roman world. His thirty-ninth Festal Letter (367) is the first list of exactly the 27 books of the New Testament as canonical. At the Council of Alexandria (362) he worked for reconciliation with the moderate homoiousians, preparing the Cappadocian settlement.

Timothy Barnes and others have shown how far Athanasius' account is partisan and that his opponents' charges of violence were not baseless. Still, his tenacity ('Athanasius against the world') and alliance with Egyptian monks and people made him the key figure of fourth-century theology. Coptic and Orthodox churches venerate him as a Father.

scholarship: Barnes, Athanasius and Constantius (1993)
Gwynn, Athanasius of Alexandria (2012)

Arius was born around 256 in Libya and may have studied at Antioch under Lucian, whose pupils he later called fellow 'Collucianists'. Ordained presbyter at Alexandria, he was in charge of the church of Baucalis, a popular preacher with an ascetic reputation. Around 318 (some scholars say c. 320-322) his teaching that the Son was created by the Father out of nothing, before time but not eternal, and that 'there was when he was not', led Bishop Alexander to condemn him. He took refuge with Eusebius of Nicomedia and wrote the Thalia, partly in verse, of which fragments survive in Athanasius, as well as letters to Eusebius and Alexander that are the best evidence of his theology. Philostorgius says he wrote songs for sailors, millers and travellers to spread his ideas.

The Council of Nicaea condemned him in 325 and Constantine exiled him to Illyricum with two Libyan bishops, ordering his books burned. Around 327-328, after submitting a vague creed, he was recalled by Constantine. Athanasius refused to readmit him in Alexandria, and the struggle over Arius' readmission became part of the campaign against Athanasius. The synod of Jerusalem in 335 received him into communion. In 336 Constantine ordered Bishop Alexander of Constantinople to admit him; on the eve of the ceremony Arius died suddenly in a public latrine in Constantinople, which Athanasius and Socrates present as divine judgement, describing his bowels pouring out.

Arius' importance lies less in his own work than in the controversy that bore his name. Modern scholars (Rowan Williams, Hanson, Gwynn) stress that 'Arianism' was a label invented by Athanasius to lump together diverse opponents, few of whom considered themselves followers of Arius. The Homoian Christianity later adopted by the Goths, Vandals and other Germanic peoples was also called Arian by their opponents.

sources.w: Letter to Serapion on the Death of Arius

scholarship: Williams, Arius: Heresy and Tradition (2nd ed., 2001)
Hanson, The Search for the Christian Doctrine of God (1988)

Eusebius was born around 260-265, probably at Caesarea Maritima in Palestine. He studied with the presbyter Pamphilus, who had built up the library founded by Origen, and took the name Eusebius Pamphili; together they wrote a Defence of Origen while Pamphilus was in prison before his martyrdom in 310. During the Great Persecution Eusebius witnessed martyrdoms in Palestine and Egypt; enemies later claimed he had escaped by sacrificing. Around 313 he became bishop of Caesarea, a position he held until his death around 339.

Eusebius was the most learned Christian scholar of his age. His Chronicle, with its parallel columns of Hebrew, Greek, Egyptian, Persian and Roman history, became, through Jerome's Latin version, the foundation of Christian chronology. The Ecclesiastical History, the first history of the church from the apostles to Constantine, quotes hundreds of documents now otherwise lost and was published in several editions between about 313 and 325. He also wrote the Martyrs of Palestine, the apologetic Preparation for the Gospel and Demonstration of the Gospel, an Onomasticon of biblical place names that is a key source for the historical geography of Palestine, the Canon tables for comparing the Gospels, and works against Porphyry, Hierocles and Marcellus of Ancyra.

In the Arian controversy Eusebius supported Arius at first and was provisionally condemned at Antioch early in 325, but at Nicaea he accepted the creed, explaining his reservations to his church. He was close to Constantine, who commissioned him to supply fifty Bibles for Constantinople, and delivered the Tricennial Oration in 336, setting out a theology of the Christian emperor as image of the divine Logos. His Life of Constantine, left unfinished at his death, is the main source and panegyric of the first Christian emperor. Timothy Barnes' Constantine and Eusebius (1981) is the fundamental study.

scholarship: Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (1981)
Johnson, Eusebius (2014)

Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus was born around 200-210 into a wealthy family of Carthage and became a celebrated teacher of rhetoric. Converted around 246 under the influence of the presbyter Caecilianus, he gave his property to the poor, wrote To Donatus describing his conversion, and was elected bishop of Carthage in 248 or 249 by popular acclaim against the opposition of some presbyters. When Decius' edict came in 250, he went into hiding and governed his church by letters, a decision that weakened his authority; confessors in prison issued certificates of forgiveness to the lapsed, and a laxist faction under Felicissimus and Novatus defied him.

Returning after Easter 251, Cyprian convened councils that established graded penance for the lapsed, rejecting both the confessors' easy pardons and the rigorism of Novatian at Rome, and wrote On the Lapsed and On the Unity of the Catholic Church, which declares that 'he cannot have God for his father who does not have the church for his mother' and that there is no salvation outside the church. During the plague he organised care for the sick of all religions and wrote On Mortality. In 255-256 he clashed with Stephen of Rome over the rebaptism of those baptised by heretics, insisting that only the true church could baptise; the 87 votes of the council of September 256 survive. More than 80 letters by or to him survive, the largest Christian correspondence of the period.

Under Valerian's first edict he was exiled to Curubis (257). Recalled after the second edict, he was tried before the proconsul Galerius Maximus and beheaded at the Ager Sexti near Carthage on 14 September 258, responding to the sentence 'Deo gratias' and giving his executioner 25 gold pieces. The Acta Proconsularia and Pontius' Life describe his death. His theology of church unity influenced both the Donatists and Augustine.

scholarship: Clarke, The Letters of St. Cyprian of Carthage I-IV (1984-89)
Brent, Cyprian and Roman Carthage (2010)

Origen was born around 185 at Alexandria into a Christian family. When his father Leonides was martyred in 202, the seventeen-year-old wanted to join him, but his mother hid his clothes. He supported his family by teaching grammar and soon took charge of catechetical instruction under Bishop Demetrius. Eusebius reports that, interpreting Matthew 19:12 literally, he castrated himself. He studied philosophy with Ammonius Saccas, teacher of Plotinus, learned Hebrew, and with the support of the wealthy Ambrosius, who provided stenographers and copyists, produced a vast body of work: Epiphanius speaks of 6,000 books. He travelled to Rome, Arabia, Greece and Antioch, where Julia Mamaea summoned him.

Ordained presbyter at Caesarea by the bishops of Palestine without Demetrius' consent, he was condemned and excluded from Alexandria around 231-232 and settled in Caesarea, where he founded a school and library; Gregory Thaumaturgus describes his teaching method in a farewell oration. His Hexapla, setting the Hebrew Old Testament beside a Greek transliteration and four Greek versions in six columns, was the greatest work of ancient textual scholarship. His On First Principles (De Principiis) was the first systematic Christian theology, speculating on the pre-existence of souls and the final restoration of all things (apokatastasis). He also wrote Against Celsus (c. 248), a rebuttal of the pagan philosopher's attack, and hundreds of commentaries and homilies, developing allegorical exegesis.

Arrested and tortured in the Decian persecution, Origen died at Tyre around 253-254 aged 69. His ideas shaped the Cappadocian Fathers, Eusebius, Jerome (before he turned against him) and monastic spirituality, but controversies over 'Origenism' in the 390s and 540s led to his condemnation in 553 under Justinian, so that much of his work survives only in Latin translations by Rufinus and Jerome.

scholarship: Crouzel, Origen (1989)
McGuckin (ed.), The Westminster Handbook to Origen (2004)
